# Tone of voice

## Who is talking, to whom

Write as **"we"**, the studio, in almost every sentence. The name "Northfold" appears only on the Home and About pages ("Northfold is a landscape and garden design studio in Northumberland"). "I" belongs only to quoted people: "I've learned more in a year here than in the five before it."

Your reader is a garden owner in the north of England, either a client or someone thinking about becoming one. Address them as **"you"** and assume they garden themselves: "If you left your borders standing over winter (and we hope you did)".

Keep the attitude relaxed and confident. Be warm without gushing and dry rather than jokey. Give firm opinions ("this is the one we'd never skip") and disagree politely ("We'd like to gently disagree"). Admit small things freely ("if we're honest", "surprised us a little too").

## How a piece is shaped

**Journal pieces** open on something concrete: a scene, a problem, or a thing people say. Examples: "This one started with a puddle." "'We haven't got room for a tree.' We hear it a lot". Then widen to the general principle and come back down to specifics under short headings.

**Case studies** follow the same arc each time. The site and the problem come first ("What they asked for"), then what we did, then a look back: "Two winters in", "A year on", "What we'd do differently".

**Endings** usually have two parts:
- A one-line saying set on its own line: "A tidy garden in winter is usually an empty one."
- A low-key offer of help: "it might be worth a conversation", "Bring wellies."

**Pages** use the same order every time: a short tagline, a one-line intro, a call to action, short sections, an image caption, then a client or staff quote with attribution ("Client, Harrogate"). They close on a question and a button: "Not sure which you need?" … "Book a consultation".

## Sentences and words

Most sentences are medium length and plain. Cut them with short ones for rhythm: "It's meant to." "Don't." "That felt right." "It's been through a lot."

Signature moves:
- **Colons that unpack an idea:** "chosen for three things: they had to be hardy…"
- **Brackets for asides:** "(or a sharp spade, if you're feeling decisive)"
- **A punchline at the end of a paragraph:** "Delphiniums would have lasted about a week."
- **Questions a client would really ask:** "Is there a dog who digs?"
- **Lists as fragments with no closing full stop:** "A fair salary, reviewed every year"

**Vocabulary** is practical and northern-domestic. Use phrases like "a lot of tea", "properly", "come good", "earns its keep", "tough as old boots", "the kettle's on". Use contractions throughout.

**Spelling** is UK: "colour", "fertiliser", "metres", "mould".

**Tense:** use the present for advice and the past for what we did on a project.

**Numbers** are mostly spelled out: "forty-two new trees", "five centimetres", "Twenty-eight days' holiday". Digits appear for years, scales and phone numbers ("1:50", "2014"), and once for a measurement ("about 30 centimetres deep"). Follow the majority and use words. Write times the way people say them: "nine until half five".

**Prices** never appear. Talk about cost in principle instead: "the cost is usually saved in plants that don't die".

**Plant names:**
- Use botanical names with cultivars in single quotes: Calamagrostis 'Karl Foerster'.
- Gloss the common name: "Crambe maritima, sea kale".

**Technical terms** get explained in passing: "yellow rattle, a semi-parasitic annual that weakens the grasses".

## Titles, summaries and headings

**Titles** are in sentence case, literal and unclever:
- Case studies: "Planting for salt and wind at Craster", "Bringing back a walled garden near Corbridge"
- Numbered lists: "Five trees for a small garden"
- Opinion pieces: "Why we leave the seedheads standing", "Meadows are not low-maintenance"

**Standfirsts** take two forms:
- A comma list of specifics: "Two years, one very old wall and a lot of bindweed."
- A plain promise: "Here's where we'd spend the time."

**Section headings** are short, in sentence case, and often a verb phrase or a plain label: "Shelter first", "Look first", "Plants that cope", "What happens next". Only "Five trees" numbers its headings.

**Page taglines** are warm and concrete: "A small studio with muddy boots", "Come and see us".

**Buttons** are plain verbs: "Get in touch", "Read the journal".

## What this voice never does

- **No exclamation marks.** None appear anywhere.
- **No sales language.** Avoid "bespoke", "passionate", "transform", "stunning", "solutions", "curated", "nestled", "dream garden".
- **No machine-written tells.** Avoid "delve", "whether you're a… or a…", "elevate", "unlock", "in today's world", "In conclusion", tidy triplets of adjectives, and summary paragraphs that repeat the headings.
- **No em dashes in running text.** Use commas, colons and full stops. The one em dash in the samples sits in a quote attribution.
- **No overpromising.** The voice punctures promises instead: "if someone tells you one will look after itself, they're selling you something."
- **No vague praise.** Always name the plant, the place or the month.

## Examples to imitate

> "Someone's grandchild planted the last tree. That felt right."

This shows the short, understated emotional beat.

> "Then we cut it down. And down again."

This shows rhythm through repetition and fragments.

> "It doesn't gust so much as lean."

This shows precise, observed description instead of adjectives.

> "Clean and sharpen your secateurs. You'll thank yourself in March."

This shows practical advice with a dry payoff.

> "A meadow isn't a lawn you've stopped mowing. It's a crop you harvest once a year."

This shows the stand-alone saying that closes a section.

> "And yes, there are still cows in the next field, so please shut the gate."

This shows the domestic, local humour.

> "Flexible hours, as long as the plants are watered"

This shows a list fragment with a light twist.

> "The drawing is the easy bit. The thinking behind it is what you're really paying for."

This shows the voice being straight about value without quoting a price.
